v.q: Two threads run `count++` on a shared `int` without synchronisation. Why can updates be lost?
o: The increment is read, add, write, so threads can overwrite each other
The JVM lets only one thread touch an int at a time
Integers are immutable, so the write is ignored
The garbage collector resets the value between threads
v.w: `count++` is three steps, not one atomic action. Use `AtomicInteger`, `LongAdder` or a lock.

v.q: Which operation is atomic on a shared int field without any synchronisation?
o: A plain read
count++
count += 2
count *= 2
v.w: A plain read or write of an int is atomic, but increments and other read-modify-write actions are not.

v.q: What does the `volatile` keyword guarantee for a field?
o: Writes are visible to other threads, but compound actions stay non-atomic
Every method touching the field becomes synchronized
The field is held in a faster CPU register only
The field can no longer change after construction
v.w: `volatile` gives visibility and ordering for single reads and writes. `volatile int x; x++` is still a race.

v.q: Which statement about volatile is NOT true?
o: It makes count++ atomic
It makes writes visible to other threads
It prevents some instruction reordering
It is enough for a simple stop flag
v.w: Volatile gives visibility and ordering, not atomicity of compound actions. Use AtomicInteger or a lock for those.

v.q: What is the main difference between `synchronized` and `ReentrantLock`?
o: `ReentrantLock` adds timeouts, interruptible waits and fairness
`synchronized` works across several JVMs, `ReentrantLock` does not
`ReentrantLock` releases itself at the end of the block
`synchronized` can guard only a single variable
v.w: `ReentrantLock` must be unlocked in a `finally` block. Prefer `synchronized` for simple cases and a lock when you need its extra features.

v.q: Which feature does synchronized NOT offer but ReentrantLock does?
o: tryLock with a timeout
Mutual exclusion
Reentrancy
Memory visibility on release
v.w: synchronized always waits. ReentrantLock can try, time out, wait interruptibly and be fair.

v.q: Two threads each hold one lock and wait forever for the other's lock. What is this called, and what is the standard prevention?
o: Deadlock; always acquire locks in one global order
Livelock; add more threads to the pool
Starvation; raise the priority of the waiting thread
Race condition; mark both locks volatile
v.w: Consistent lock ordering removes the circular wait. Also keep critical sections small and use timeouts such as `tryLock`.

v.q: Which measure is NOT a way to prevent deadlock?
o: Hold each lock for as long as possible
Acquire locks in a global order
Use tryLock with a timeout
Hold fewer locks at once
v.w: Longer holding increases the chance of a cycle. Ordering, timeouts and fewer locks reduce it.

v.q: You submit 10,000 short tasks. Which approach is the most sensible?
o: A bounded thread pool from an `ExecutorService`
A brand new `Thread` for each of the tasks
One `synchronized` method that runs them all
A `Thread.sleep` between every submission
v.w: Pools reuse threads and cap resource use. Unbounded thread creation can exhaust memory and slow the whole JVM.

v.q: Why is creating a new Thread for every request a poor design?
o: Threads are costly and the count is unbounded
Threads cannot run Runnable objects
Threads cannot share memory
The JVM allows only 10 threads
v.w: A bounded pool reuses threads, limits memory and protects the system from overload.

o: Transforms the result when it arrives, without blocking the caller
Blocks until the future completes and returns the value
Cancels the future when it takes too long
Runs the stage again every time it is called
v.w: It chains non-blocking steps. `get()` and `join()` are the blocking calls. Pass your own executor to avoid saturating the common pool.

v.q: Which CompletableFuture method combines the results of two independent futures?
o: thenCombine
thenApply
join
cancel
v.w: thenCombine takes two futures and a function over both results. thenApply works on one result.

v.q: Why is `ConcurrentHashMap` preferred over `Collections.synchronizedMap` for heavy concurrent use?
o: It locks only small parts of the map, so contention drops
It keeps keys in sorted order for quicker lookups
It permits `null` keys and values to skip checks
It never needs to resize as it grows
v.w: A synchronized wrapper uses one lock for every call. `ConcurrentHashMap` uses CAS and fine-grained locking per bin. It rejects `null` keys and values.

v.q: Which statement about ConcurrentHashMap is NOT true?
o: All operations take a single global lock
Reads do not block
Writers lock only a part of the table
It does not allow null keys
v.w: It was designed to avoid a global lock, which is what Collections.synchronizedMap uses.

v.q: A task in a thread pool throws an exception inside `Runnable.run()` submitted with `execute()`. What typically happens?
o: The worker thread dies from the exception and the pool replaces it
The exception is rethrown to the code that called `execute`
The pool shuts itself down at once
The task is silently retried three times
v.w: With `submit()` the exception is captured inside the `Future` and only appears on `get()`. Always handle or log task failures.

v.q: How do you see an exception thrown by a task submitted with submit() to an ExecutorService?
o: Call get() on the returned Future
Wrap submit in try and catch
Read the pool log file
Call shutdown()
v.w: submit captures the exception in the Future. get() rethrows it wrapped in ExecutionException.
